title: How Colleagues Are Terminated Really Matters
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Admired Leadership argues that the mechanics of firing someone are not an HR back-office matter but one of the loudest signals a leader ever sends. The piece frames termination as a symbolic act, read closely by the people who remain, that either confirms or exposes the values an organization claims on its walls. It dismisses the standard corporate anesthetic — that layoffs are business, not personal — as a self-serving fiction available only to leaders who treat colleagues as interchangeable. The argument turns on the ripple effect: because departing colleagues carry long friendships inside the building, every exit is felt personally by many people at once. Practically, the author insists a graceful exit process is not technically difficult, and that the golden rule is a sufficient design specification. The closing move groups termination with promotion and compensation as the three acts that carry disproportionate meaning, making the handling of exits a durable test of a leader's credibility.
points: The piece's sharpest claim is that remaining employees read a termination as a forecast of their own treatment, which makes exit procedure a culture-setting act rather than an administrative one.
Blindsiding people, staging bogus meetings, and walk-outs under escort are named as the specific practices that broadcast the wrong message to stakeholders inside and outside the organization.
The author flatly rejects the 'it's not personal, it's business' defense as available only to leaders who regard team members as fungible.
A useful design test is offered: treating people as you would want to be treated is enough to build a respectful exit process, so difficulty is never the real excuse.
Termination is grouped with promotion and compensation as the three 'lightning rods of meaning' — the acts where stated values are either proven or exposed.
quotes: Good leaders know that how people are terminated is a hugely symbolic act that reflects the true values of the organization and its leaders. Those colleagues who remain maintain a watchful eye, knowing the same treatment could be applied to them.

This means the consequences of terminating colleagues have a ripple effect on relationships throughout the organization. This makes every termination highly personal, even when the reason for dismissal is a layoff or reduction in force (the so-called RIF in large enterprises).
The idea that layoffs are a business decision and not personal is ludicrous. Only leaders who see team members as fungible and expendable would make such a case.
Designing a respectful and graceful exit process is not that hard. Treating people like you would want to be treated is the best guide.

Explaining away the legitimate needs of those on the way out by insinuating that everyone knows this is how business works is a cop out. Organizations and leaders who say they lead with values such as respect, integrity, and inclusion must prove it in every circumstance, not just in team forums and on-wall displays.

The best leaders know some leadership acts carry huge symbolic weight. Promotion, compensation, and termination are the lightning rods of meaning in every organization. How team members are terminated carries long-term implications for leaders.
